name: Boost.Charconv
workload: Round-trip shortest to_chars/from_chars formatting and parsing of float/double and base-10 uint32_t/uint64_t integers, scored relative to std::printf/std::strtoX, on GCC 13.1 (Linux), MSVC 14.3 (Windows), and GCC 13.2 (macOS ARM).
claimed_speedup: Relative-to-printf scores: double to_chars 6.20x (Boost) vs 6.03x (std::to_chars) on Linux GCC13.1; float to_chars 4.46x vs 4.01x; double from_chars 5.75x vs 5.77x (near tie); uint64 to_chars on Windows MSVC 2.06x (Boost) vs 2.10x (std, Boost slightly slower); ARM macOS double to_chars 6.86x vs 6.47x. Overall: at least as fast as std::to_chars/from_chars, up to ~1.3x faster in most cases, with a few near-ties or slight regressions.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.1.0 on Ubuntu 23.04 (b2 cxxstd=20, release); MSVC 14.3 (V17.7.0) on Windows 11; Homebrew GCC 13.2.0 on macOS Ventura 13.5.2 (M1 Pro, ARM)
hardware: x86_64 Linux (unspecified CPU model); x86_64 Windows (unspecified CPU model); Apple M1 Pro (ARM macOS)
stars_or_usage: 32 stars; part of the Boost C++ Libraries collection
tradeoffs: Wraps/duplicates functionality already in C++17 <charconv>; main value is C++11 portability and marginal speed; requires Boost; benchmark run and maintained by the library's own authors (not independent third party).
caveats: Not a uniform large win — several results are near-ties or slight regressions vs std (e.g. Windows uint64 to_chars: 2.06x Boost vs 2.10x std). Numbers come from the maintainers' own in-repo benchmark, not an independent third party, though methodology, compiler, and hardware are all disclosed and the benchmark is reproducible via `-a release` b2 build.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "Boost.Charconv faster than std::to_chars benchmark" -> github.com/boostorg/charconv; numbers confirmed by reading doc/charconv/benchmarks.adoc via gh api

name: c4core (charconv/xtoa/atox module)
workload: CI-run microbenchmarks (c4::xtoa/c4::atox) converting 8/16/32/64-bit signed and unsigned integers and floats to/from decimal ASCII strings, measured in MB/s, against std::to_chars/std::from_chars, sprintf/scanf, and stringstream, on Linux (g++11.2, GCC12.1 charts) and Windows (VS2019).
claimed_speedup: xtoa (formatting): ~40% to 2x faster than std::to_chars(); ~10x-30x faster than sprintf(); ~50x-100x faster than naive stringstream operator<<+str(). atox (parsing): ~10%-30% faster than std::from_chars(); ~10x faster than scanf(); ~30x-50x faster than naive stringstream str()+operator>>. (Stated for a Linux/g++11.2 run; per-platform MB/s charts also published for Linux GCC12.1 and Windows VS2019.)
compiler_and_flags: g++ 11.2 (text claim) / g++ 12.1 Release (Linux charts); MSVC / VS2019 Release (Windows charts); exact optimization flags not shown in README prose
tradeoffs: Part of a large general-purpose C++ utility library, not a standalone charconv package; when compiled with C++17 and the fast_float path enabled, float/double from_chars performance rides on bundled fast_float (github.com/fastfloat/fast_float, already catalogued) as a dependency — the integer xtoa/atox path is c4core's own code, the float path is not entirely original.
caveats: Numbers are from the project's own README/CI benchmark runs, not independently verified by a third party; the 40%-2x vs std::to_chars figure is stated for one Linux/GCC11.2 run in prose, while the Windows/Linux GCC12.1 charts are images (PNG) whose exact numeric deltas were not extracted as text this session — only the prose percentages were confirmed as literal page text.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "c4core charconv benchmark iostream faster" -> github.com/biojppm/c4core; performance claim and percentages confirmed in README.md via gh api raw fetch

name: fast_double_parser
workload: Parsing arrays of random-integer-valued doubles and real-world geographic-coordinate doubles (canada.json) from text into IEEE754 double, measured in MB/s, against strtod on Apple clang / Intel i7-7700K.
claimed_speedup: Headline: 4x faster than strtod. Benchmark detail: random integers 460.64 MB/s (fast_double_parser) vs 186.90 MB/s (strtod), ~2.5x; canada.json real-world doubles 662.01 MB/s vs 69.73 MB/s, ~9.5x.
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang (exact version/flags not confirmed this session)
stars_or_usage: 670 stars; algorithm ported into Go's standard library and used in Microsoft LightGBM
tradeoffs: Only parses double (no formatting direction); JSON (RFC 7159) grammar only, not the full strtod grammar (e.g. no hex floats); superseded by the same author's fast_float (github.com/fastfloat/fast_float, already catalogued), which the README itself now recommends instead.
caveats: The project's own README explicitly tells users to adopt fast_float instead ('We encourage users to adopt fast_float library instead of fast_double_parser'), so this is best treated as a historical/reference implementation rather than a current recommendation; benchmarked directly against strtod (the C routine std::stod delegates to) rather than a literal std::stod(std::string) call, though the two are computationally equivalent for this purpose.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "lemire fast_double_parser benchmark strtod" -> github.com/lemire/fast_double_parser; numbers confirmed via WebFetch of repo README/benchmarks

name: fast_io
workload: Writing and re-reading 10 million sequential integers to/from a file, and separately writing 10 million doubles with round-trip Ryu-based formatting, measured in wall-clock seconds, against std::fstream/stdio/boost::iostreams and, for the double case, MSVC's std::to_chars.
claimed_speedup: Integer I/O: fast_io::obuf_file output ~6-10x faster than std::fstream (e.g. Linux GCC11: fstream-with-sputc-trick 0.319s vs fast_io 0.050s; MinGW-W64 GCC11: fstream 0.462s vs fast_io 0.049s). Double formatting: 'fast_io defeats msvc's charconv (std::to_chars) for over 20%' on MSVC 19.26 (i/obuf_file 0.465s vs std::to_chars+obuf_file 0.601s, ~22.6% faster).
compiler_and_flags: MinGW-W64 GCC 11.0.0; MSVC 19.26.28805; GCC 11.0.0 with glibc+libstdc++ (Linux); optimization flags not stated in the tables
tradeoffs: Uses a non-standard, non-OSI-approved 'Anti-Tivo License' with unusual conditional-GPLv3 clauses rather than a conventional permissive/copyleft license; large paradigm shift from <iostream> (not a drop-in replacement, requires C++20 concepts); the original repository was archived once already due to git history bloat.
caveats: No CPU/hardware model is stated in any benchmark table (only OS and compiler versions), which falls short of Tier A's full compiler+flags+hardware disclosure, so this is capped at B; the numbers are the author's own README claims, not independently reproduced this session, and results vary noticeably between the two Windows runs shown (MinGW vs MSVC) and the Linux run.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "c4core charconv benchmark iostream faster" surfaced cppfastio/fast_io; benchmark tables confirmed via gh api raw fetch of readme.md

name: CharConv.h (rigtorp)
workload: Converting base-10 32/64-bit signed/unsigned integers to and from strings across 1-9 digit lengths, measured in nanoseconds per call via Google Benchmark, against sprintf, std::to_string, std::stringstream, atoi, strtol, and std::stoi.
claimed_speedup: Own to_chars: 9-20ns vs sprintf 73-87ns (~4-8x), std::to_string 76-90ns (~4-8x), std::stringstream 34-55ns (~2-4x). Own from_chars (checked): 9-19ns vs atoi/strtol 14-28ns and std::stoi 16-29ns (~1.5-2x); unchecked variant 4-10ns (~3-4x faster than atoi/strtol).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (Google Benchmark output shown; compiler/optimization flags absent from README)
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2620 v4 @ 2.10GHz, 32 cores, L1 32K/L2 256K/L3 20480K caches
tradeoffs: Only base-10 32/64-bit signed/unsigned integers, no floating point; its own to_chars/from_chars functions have an API 'similar, but not identical' to std::to_chars/std::from_chars — this repo does not itself call or benchmark the actual std::to_chars/std::from_chars functions, only stringstream/to_string/atoi/strtol/stoi.
caveats: Benchmark is dated 2017-12-26 (pre-dates widely-available std::to_chars/from_chars implementations), and compiler/optimization flags are not disclosed, only hardware — so despite having a real, reproducible in-repo benchmark, it is capped below Tier A. No direct std::to_chars/std::from_chars comparison was found in this repo; baseline recorded reflects what was actually benchmarked (stringstream/to_string/atoi/strtol/stoi).
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "rigtorp CharConv benchmark integer string conversion" -> github.com/rigtorp/CharConv; full benchmark table confirmed via gh api raw fetch of README.md

name: jeaiii/itoa
baseline: integer-to-string formatting (best guess: std::to_chars); direct evidence found only vs {fmt}'s integer formatter
workload: Converting integers to decimal ASCII strings across all digit lengths with uniform-random values and uniform-random digit lengths, benchmarked in an author-run, self-described debug-mode Google Benchmark on Compiler Explorer/godbolt against the {fmt} library's integer formatter.
claimed_speedup: BM_jea 10.2ns vs BM_fmt 16.6ns (~1.6x faster), per the README's godbolt comparison. Author also claims the current version is '25% faster' than an earlier version of the same algorithm, per the classic miloyip/itoa-benchmark harness (which itself only measures against sprintf/naive/lut/sse2-style itoa variants, not std::to_chars).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC/VS2019 for the digit-length testing claim; the {fmt} comparison used Google Benchmark 'compiled in debug' per the author's own disclaimer
stars_or_usage: 254 stars; algorithm write-up by dragonbox author Junekey Jeon; widely referenced across itoa benchmark shootouts (miloyip/itoa-benchmark, TobiSchluter/itoa-benchmark forks)
tradeoffs: Integers only, no floating point; single header, no dependencies; the classic itoa-benchmark shootout this project descends from (miloyip/itoa-benchmark) predates C++17 and explicitly disables the C++ standard-library competitors (ostringstream/to_string) by default, and neither it nor jeaiii/itoa's own README includes a std::to_chars comparison.
caveats: The only in-repo numeric comparison (vs {fmt}) is explicitly disclaimed by the author as unreliable because Google Benchmark was compiled in debug mode; per the hard rule for debug-build benchmarks this is capped at Tier C. No verified head-to-head vs std::to_chars was located this session despite checking the linked itoa-benchmark and its forks. Included at low confidence because it is a widely-cited reference algorithm for this exact task (integer-to-string), valuable for the research/reference tier even though direct std comparison evidence is currently weak.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "jeaiii itoa fastest integer to string conversion github" -> github.com/jeaiii/itoa; cross-checked against github.com/miloyip/itoa-benchmark and github.com/jeaiii/itoa-benchmark via gh api raw README fetches
